facts.text: Molecular-dynamics uniaxial tensile loading was applied along the <110>, <1-12>, and <-111> crystallographic directions.
The tensile simulations varied temperature among 10 K, 300 K, and 600 K.
The tensile simulations varied strain rate among 10^8, 10^9, and 10^10 s^-1.
The model was annealed by heating it to 1000 K, holding it there, and cooling it to 300 K before tensile testing.
Temperature was controlled with a Nose–Hoover thermostat using a 1 fs molecular-dynamics time step.
Yielding began with dislocation nucleation at vacancy clusters or locally disordered atoms and coincided with a sudden stress drop.
Plastic flow was mediated by 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations that generated intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults.
The stacking faults produced local HCP-like atomic regions without a bulk phase transformation.
Increasing temperature enhanced thermal vibrations, facilitated dislocation nucleation, and lowered the critical resolved shear stress.
The <-111> loading orientation exhibited the highest yield stress among the three tested orientations.
Yield strength decreased as temperature increased, but showed negligible sensitivity to strain rate across 10^8–10^10 s^-1.
Higher strain rates increased dislocation density and flow stress, while neither FCC-to-BCC transformation nor deformation twinning was observed.
